planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons; KSU-Dunnigan needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: KSU-Dunnigan is one of the more recent releases from Kentucky State University's pawpaw breeding program, selected for a mid-to-late ripening window that follows earlier KSU selections. Fruit runs medium in size with a low seed-to-flesh ratio and creamy flesh carrying a tropical mango-pineapple-banana flavor profile typical of well-regarded named pawpaws. Grow it like other pawpaws, starting young trees in partial shade before moving them toward full sun as they mature, and keep soil consistently moist through establishment since the shallow root system is intolerant of drought. Plant a second, unrelated named cultivar nearby, since pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen.
sources: Kentucky State University School of Agriculture, Communities, and the Environment — Pawpaw Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for best fruiting; KSU-Pomper's Choice needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: KSU-Pomper's Choice is a Kentucky State University pawpaw selection, formerly tracked under a numbered breeding designation, prized for plump, freestone fruit whose seeds separate cleanly from the thick custardy flesh. The flavor leans toward a sweet mango-pineapple-banana blend, and fruit ripens in the mid-to-late season window shared with several other KSU releases. Unlike many pawpaws that tolerate partial shade reasonably well, this selection is noted as needing full sun for best production, so site it accordingly. Keep young trees consistently watered through their first two seasons and interplant with an unrelated named cultivar for pollination, since pawpaw is self-incompatible.
sources: Kentucky State University School of Agriculture, Communities, and the Environment — Pawpaw Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons; October Moon is a late-ripening selection that extends the pawpaw harvest window into early October in many regions.

directions: October Moon is a late-ripening pawpaw selection bred by the late Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana, valued for carrying the pawpaw season further into fall than most named cultivars. The vigorous, heavy-bearing tree produces very large fruit with dense, creamy, melting flesh and relatively few seeds, with banana and mango notes dominating the flavor. Grow it like other pawpaws in moist, humus-rich soil, starting young trees in partial shade before moving them toward full sun as they mature. Plant a second, genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since this species will not set fruit from its own pollen.
sources: Kentucky State University School of Agriculture, Communities, and the Environment — Pawpaw Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons; Benny's Favorite ripens mid-to-late season and needs an unrelated pawpaw cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Benny's Favorite is a pawpaw selection from a cross of 'Prolific' and a Sam Norris seedling, bred by the late Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana. Fruit is medium-sized with smooth, creamy texture and a sweet, well-balanced flavor often described as especially true to classic pawpaw character. Grow it like other pawpaws in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, starting young trees in partial shade before transitioning them toward fuller sun as they mature. Interplant with a genetically distinct cultivar for cross-pollination and keep soil consistently moist through the first two seasons while the shallow root system establishes.
sources: Pawpaw grower and nursery cultivar records (growing-pawpaw.webnode.page)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jerry's Big Girl is a vigorous, fast-growing selection that tends to bear earlier than many other named cultivars.

directions: Jerry's Big Girl is a pawpaw selection from a cross of 'Sunflower' and a Sam Norris seedling, bred by the late Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana, and is consistently noted for producing an unusually high share of very large fruit, some reaching a pound or more. Flesh carries a peach-and-banana-leaning flavor and the fruit ripens in the mid-to-late season. The tree itself is notably vigorous and fast to establish compared with many other named selections, making it a strong anchor tree for a new planting. Grow it in moist, humus-rich soil with young trees in partial shade, transitioning to full sun at maturity, and plant a genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
sources: Pawpaw grower and nursery cultivar records (growing-pawpaw.webnode.page)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil; VE-21 is a very-early-ripening selection useful for shorter-season northern gardens, and it needs a genetically distinct cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: VE-21, also known as Valley East 21, is a pawpaw selection from a cross of 'Prolific' and 'Overleese' bred by the late Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana, chosen specifically for its very early ripening, which can extend the usable pawpaw season in cooler climates. Fruit ranges from average to large with light yellow, soft, creamy flesh and a sweet, classic pawpaw flavor. Grow it like other pawpaws in moist, humus-rich soil, starting young trees in partial shade before moving them toward full sun as they mature. Plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, and keep soil consistently moist through establishment.
sources: Pawpaw grower and nursery cultivar records (growing-pawpaw.webnode.page)
